title: Thermodynamics & Kinetics
description: Calorimetry, Hess's law, formation enthalpies, entropy, ΔG with K and E°, rate laws, first-order half-life, Arrhenius, mechanisms and catalysts.

cards.title: What is the specific heat capacity of liquid water, as a number in J/(g·°C)?
cards.body:
4.184

The value is the same per kelvin, and equals 1 cal/(g·°C).

Example: $q = mc\Delta T$, so warming $50.0\,\mathrm{g}$ of water by $10.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ takes $50.0 \times 4.184 \times 10.0 = 2.09\,\mathrm{kJ}$.
Watch out: ice and steam have about **half** this value, so don't reuse 4.184 for them.
cards.searchQuery: specific heat capacity of water 4.184 J/g°C

cards.title: During a reaction in a coffee-cup calorimeter, the water's temperature rises. What is the sign of $\Delta H$ for the reaction?
cards.body:
Negative: the reaction is **exothermic**.

Heat released by the system is absorbed by the solution, so $q_{\mathrm{rxn}} = -q_{\mathrm{soln}} = -mc\Delta T$.

An endothermic reaction ($\Delta H > 0$) would make the solution colder.

Key idea: at constant pressure, $\Delta H = q$.
cards.searchQuery: coffee cup calorimeter temperature rise exothermic sign of delta H

cards.title: $\ce{A + B -> C}$ has $\Delta H = -100\,\mathrm{kJ}$. What is $\Delta H$ in kJ for $\ce{2C -> 2A + 2B}$?
cards.body:
+200

Hess's law: enthalpy is a **state function**, so $\Delta H$ values add along any path.

Reversing a reaction flips the sign of $\Delta H$; multiplying its coefficients by $n$ multiplies $\Delta H$ by $n$.

Example: reverse ($+100$), then double ($+200$).
cards.searchQuery: Hess's law reverse reaction multiply coefficients enthalpy change

cards.title: $\Delta H^\circ_f$ (kJ/mol): $\ce{CH4(g)}$ $-74.6$, $\ce{CO2(g)}$ $-393.5$, $\ce{H2O(l)}$ $-285.8$. What is $\Delta H^\circ$ in kJ for $\ce{CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O(l)}$?
cards.body:
-890.5

$\Delta H^\circ_{\mathrm{rxn}} = \sum n\Delta H^\circ_f(\text{products}) - \sum n\Delta H^\circ_f(\text{reactants}) = [-393.5 + 2(-285.8)] - [-74.6 + 0]$.

$\ce{O2(g)}$ is an element in its standard state, so its $\Delta H^\circ_f = 0$.

Watch out: products minus reactants (not the reverse), and keep the coefficient 2.
cards.searchQuery: standard enthalpy of combustion methane from enthalpy of formation

cards.title: Predict the sign of $\Delta S^\circ$ for $\ce{2SO2(g) + O2(g) -> 2SO3(g)}$.
cards.body:
Negative: 3 mol of gas become 2 mol.

Entropy increases with more moles of gas, solid to liquid to gas, higher temperature, larger volume, dissolving a solid, and more complex molecules.

Tip: a change in the **moles of gas** usually dominates.
cards.searchQuery: predict sign of entropy change moles of gas SO2 SO3

cards.title: $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$. If $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S < 0$, when is the process spontaneous?
cards.body:
Only at **low temperatures** (below $T = \Delta H/\Delta S$).

All four cases:
- $\Delta H -$, $\Delta S +$: always
- $\Delta H +$, $\Delta S -$: never
- $\Delta H -$, $\Delta S -$: low $T$
- $\Delta H +$, $\Delta S +$: high $T$

Example: water freezing ($\Delta H < 0$, $\Delta S < 0$) is spontaneous only below $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
cards.searchQuery: Gibbs free energy spontaneity four cases enthalpy entropy temperature

cards.title: At $298\,\mathrm{K}$ a reaction has $\Delta G^\circ = -11.4\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. Estimate $K$ using $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$.
cards.body:
100

$\ln K = 11{,}400 \div (8.314 \times 298) \approx 4.6$, and $e^{4.6} \approx 100$.

Tip: at $298\,\mathrm{K}$, every $-5.7\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ multiplies $K$ by 10.
Watch out: use $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$ here, not 0.08206, and convert kJ to J.
cards.searchQuery: delta G standard to equilibrium constant K = e^(-ΔG/RT)

cards.title: What is the Faraday constant $F$, used in $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ$, as a number in coulombs per mole of electrons?
cards.body:
96485

$n$ is the moles of electrons transferred, and $1\,\mathrm{C\cdot V} = 1\,\mathrm{J}$. Positive $E^\circ$ means negative $\Delta G^\circ$: a spontaneous (galvanic) cell.

Example: Zn/Cu cell, $n = 2$, $E^\circ = 1.10\,\mathrm{V}$: $\Delta G^\circ = -2 \times 96{,}485 \times 1.10\,\mathrm{J} \approx -212\,\mathrm{kJ}$.
cards.searchQuery: Faraday constant 96485 C/mol delta G nFE

cards.title: $\ce{2NO(g) + 2H2(g) -> N2(g) + 2H2O(g)}$ has rate $= k[\ce{NO}]^2[\ce{H2}]$. Why isn't the exponent on $\ce{H2}$ equal to its coefficient, 2?
cards.body:
Rate laws are found by **experiment**; coefficients give the orders only for a single elementary step.

This reaction occurs in several steps, and the slow step (with any steps before it) sets the orders.

Tip: find the orders from data, for example with the method of initial rates.
cards.searchQuery: rate law determined experimentally not from stoichiometry NO H2

cards.title: Holding $[\ce{B}]$ constant, doubling $[\ce{A}]$ makes the initial rate four times faster. What is the reaction order in A?
cards.body:
2

Rate ratio = (concentration ratio)$^{\text{order}}$, so $2^n = 4$ and $n = 2$: **second order**.

Doubling $[\ce{A}]$ with no rate change means zero order; rate doubles means first order; rate $\times 8$ means third order.
cards.searchQuery: method of initial rates reaction order doubling concentration

cards.title: A first-order reaction has $k = 0.0693\,\mathrm{min^{-1}}$. What is its half-life in minutes?
cards.body:
10.0

$t_{1/2} = \ln 2/k = 0.693/k$, **independent** of the starting concentration.

Each half-life halves whatever is left: 100% to 50% to 25% to 12.5%.

Watch out: zero- and second-order half-lives do depend on $[\ce{A}]_0$.
cards.searchQuery: first-order half-life ln2/k calculation

cards.title: Which plot gives a straight line for a first-order reaction, and what is its slope?
cards.body:
$\ln[\ce{A}]$ versus time, with slope $= -k$

It comes from the integrated rate law $\ln[\ce{A}]_t = -kt + \ln[\ce{A}]_0$.

Compare:
- zero order: $[\ce{A}]$ vs $t$, slope $-k$
- second order: $1/[\ce{A}]$ vs $t$, slope $+k$
cards.searchQuery: first order integrated rate law ln[A] versus time slope -k

cards.title: Arrhenius plot: what is the slope of $\ln k$ versus $1/T$?
cards.body:
$-E_a/R$

Taking the log of $k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}$ gives $\ln k = -\dfrac{E_a}{R}\left(\dfrac{1}{T}\right) + \ln A$, a straight line.

So $E_a = -\text{slope} \times 8.314\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$.

Tip: two-point form: $\ln\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{R}\left(\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right)$.
cards.searchQuery: Arrhenius plot slope ln k vs 1/T equals -Ea/R

cards.title: Mechanism: $\ce{NO2 + NO2 -> NO3 + NO}$ (slow), then $\ce{NO3 + CO -> NO2 + CO2}$ (fast). What is the rate law?
cards.body:
Rate $= k[\ce{NO2}]^2$

The slow, **rate-determining step** controls the overall rate, and for an elementary step the coefficients give the orders.

CO reacts only after the slow step, so the reaction is zero order in CO. $\ce{NO3}$ is an intermediate.

Key idea: the slowest step is the bottleneck.
cards.searchQuery: rate law from mechanism slow step NO2 CO

cards.title: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by lowering what?
cards.body:
The activation energy ($E_a$)

It provides a different mechanism with a lower barrier, speeding the forward and reverse reactions **equally**.

It doesn't change $\Delta H$, $\Delta G^\circ$, $K$ or the equilibrium yield, and it isn't consumed.
cards.searchQuery: catalyst lowers activation energy reaction rate

cards.title: What is the difference between heat and temperature?
cards.body:
**Heat** is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; **temperature** measures the average kinetic energy of the particles.

Heat flows from the hotter object to the colder one until their temperatures match.

Example: a bathtub of warm water holds far more thermal energy than a hot spoon, though the spoon is at a higher temperature.

Watch out: temperature is not the same as the total thermal energy of an object.
cards.searchQuery: difference between heat and temperature thermal energy transfer

cards.title: What is the sign of $\Delta H$ for an endothermic process?
cards.body:
positive

An **endothermic** process absorbs heat from the surroundings, so the surroundings get colder and $\Delta H > 0$.

Example: melting ice and dissolving $\ce{NH4NO3}$ in water are endothermic.

Mnemonic: endo = in; heat goes **in**, so $\Delta H$ is plus.
cards.searchQuery: endothermic process positive enthalpy change heat absorbed

cards.title: Which of these is not a state function: internal energy $U$, enthalpy $H$, entropy $S$ or work $w$?
cards.body:
Work ($w$)

A **state function** depends only on the current state of the system, not on the path taken. Heat $q$ and work $w$ both depend on the path.

Their sum is path independent: $\Delta U = q + w$.

Key idea: $\Delta$ of a state function is final minus initial, which is why Hess's law works.
cards.searchQuery: state function versus path function work heat internal energy

cards.title: How much heat, in kJ, is needed to warm $100.0\,\mathrm{g}$ of water from $20.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $35.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$? Use three significant figures.
cards.body:
6.28

$q = mc\Delta T = (100.0\,\mathrm{g})(4.184\,\mathrm{J/(g\cdot ^\circ C)})(15.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}) = 6276\,\mathrm{J}$.

Watch out: divide by 1000 to convert joules to kilojoules.
cards.searchQuery: heat required to warm water q = mcΔT calculation

cards.title: $50.0\,\mathrm{g}$ of water at $80.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ is mixed with $50.0\,\mathrm{g}$ of water at $20.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in an insulated cup. What is the final temperature in $^\circ\mathrm{C}$?
cards.body:
50.0

Heat lost by the hot water equals heat gained by the cold water: $m c(80.0 - T_f) = m c(T_f - 20.0)$.

With equal masses the result is the average of the two temperatures.

Tip: with unequal masses, use the mass-weighted average.
cards.searchQuery: calorimetry mixing hot and cold water final temperature

cards.title: $50.0\,\mathrm{mL}$ each of $1.00\,\mathrm{M}$ $\ce{HCl}$ and $\ce{NaOH}$ mix, warming $100.0\,\mathrm{g}$ of solution by $6.80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. What is $\Delta H$ (kJ per mol water formed)?
cards.body:
-56.9

$q_{\mathrm{soln}} = (100.0)(4.184)(6.80) = 2845\,\mathrm{J}$, and $0.0500\,\mathrm{mol}$ of water forms.

$\Delta H = -2845\,\mathrm{J} / 0.0500\,\mathrm{mol} = -56.9\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

Watch out: the sign is negative, because the solution gained the heat the reaction released.
cards.searchQuery: coffee cup calorimetry neutralization enthalpy HCl NaOH calculation

cards.title: A bomb calorimeter has a heat capacity of $4.50\,\mathrm{kJ/^\circ C}$, and a combustion raises its temperature by $2.00\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. How much heat, in kJ, did the reaction release?
cards.body:
9.00

$q_{\mathrm{cal}} = C_{\mathrm{cal}}\Delta T = (4.50)(2.00) = 9.00\,\mathrm{kJ}$, and the reaction released that much.

The calorimeter constant covers the water, steel and all other parts.

Tip: divide by the moles burned to get the molar heat of combustion.
cards.searchQuery: bomb calorimeter heat capacity calculation heat of combustion

cards.title: A bomb calorimeter operates at constant volume. Which quantity does the measured heat equal: $\Delta U$ or $\Delta H$?
cards.body:
$\Delta U$

At constant volume no $P\Delta V$ work is done, so $q_V = \Delta U$.

Convert to enthalpy with $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_{\mathrm{gas}}RT$ (the two differ only when the moles of gas change).

Key idea: coffee cup (constant $P$) gives $\Delta H$; bomb (constant $V$) gives $\Delta U$.
cards.searchQuery: bomb calorimeter constant volume measures internal energy change

cards.title: The first law gives $\Delta U$ in terms of heat $q$ and work $w$. Write it, with $w > 0$ meaning work done on the system.
cards.body:
$\Delta U = q + w$

Heat absorbed by the system and work done **on** the system both raise its internal energy.

Watch out: some textbooks define $w$ as work done by the system and write $\Delta U = q - w$; check your sign convention.
cards.searchQuery: first law of thermodynamics delta U equals q plus w sign convention

cards.title: A gas expands by $2.00\,\mathrm{L}$ against a constant external pressure of $1.00\,\mathrm{atm}$. What is $w$ in joules? ($1\,\mathrm{L\,atm} = 101.3\,\mathrm{J}$.)
cards.body:
-203

$w = -P_{\mathrm{ext}}\Delta V = -(1.00\,\mathrm{atm})(2.00\,\mathrm{L}) = -2.00\,\mathrm{L\,atm} = -203\,\mathrm{J}$.

The sign is negative because the system does work **on** the surroundings, lowering its energy.
cards.searchQuery: pressure-volume work w = -PΔV expansion calculation joules

cards.title: How are $\Delta H$ and $\Delta U$ related for a reaction at constant temperature involving gases?
cards.body:
$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_{\mathrm{gas}}RT$

$\Delta n_{\mathrm{gas}}$ is moles of gaseous products minus gaseous reactants, and $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$.

Example: $\ce{2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l)}$ has $\Delta n = -3$, so $\Delta H$ is more negative than $\Delta U$.

Watch out: if $\Delta n_{\mathrm{gas}} = 0$, then $\Delta H = \Delta U$.
cards.searchQuery: relationship enthalpy and internal energy delta H delta U delta n RT

cards.title: $\ce{2H2(g) + O2(g) -> 2H2O(l)}$ has $\Delta H = -572\,\mathrm{kJ}$. How much heat, in kJ, is released when $1.00\,\mathrm{mol}$ of $\ce{H2}$ burns?
cards.body:
286

The equation as written uses 2 mol of $\ce{H2}$, so 1 mol releases half: $572/2 = 286\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

Tip: $\Delta H$ is per mole of reaction **as written**, so scale it by the actual moles over the coefficient.
cards.searchQuery: thermochemical equation scaling heat released moles of hydrogen

cards.title: What conditions define the thermodynamic standard state for a gas and for a solute?
cards.body:
Gas: partial pressure of **1 bar** (nearly 1 atm). Solute: concentration of **1 M**.

A pure solid or liquid is in its pure form at 1 bar. The degree sign in $\Delta H^\circ$ marks these conditions.

Watch out: temperature is not part of the definition, though tables are usually given at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ ($298.15\,\mathrm{K}$).
cards.searchQuery: thermodynamic standard state conditions 1 bar 1 M definition

cards.title: Which has $\Delta H^\circ_f = 0$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $\ce{Br2(g)}$, $\ce{Br2(l)}$, $\ce{C}$(diamond) or $\ce{O3(g)}$?
cards.body:
$\ce{Br2(l)}$

$\Delta H^\circ_f$ is zero for an element in its **most stable form** at 1 bar and the given temperature. Bromine is a liquid at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Diamond and ozone are not the most stable forms of carbon and oxygen (graphite and $\ce{O2}$ are), so their values are not zero.
cards.searchQuery: standard enthalpy of formation zero elements standard state bromine liquid

cards.title: Write the formation reaction whose enthalpy is $\Delta H^\circ_f$ of $\ce{NaCl(s)}$.
cards.body:
$\ce{Na(s) + 1/2Cl2(g) -> NaCl(s)}$

A formation reaction makes **exactly 1 mol** of the compound from its elements in their standard states.

That's why fractional coefficients (here $\tfrac12$) are allowed.

Watch out: don't write $\ce{Cl(g)}$; chlorine's standard state is $\ce{Cl2(g)}$.
cards.searchQuery: formation reaction NaCl elements in standard states one mole

cards.title: Given $\ce{C + O2 -> CO2}$ ($-393.5\,\mathrm{kJ}$) and $\ce{CO + 1/2O2 -> CO2}$ ($-283.0\,\mathrm{kJ}$), what is $\Delta H$ in kJ for $\ce{C + 1/2O2 -> CO}$?
cards.body:
-110.5

Keep the first equation and **reverse** the second ($+283.0$), then add: $-393.5 + 283.0 = -110.5$.

The $\ce{CO2}$ cancels, leaving the target reaction.

Tip: check each species cancels or lands on the right side before adding the $\Delta H$ values.
cards.searchQuery: Hess's law carbon monoxide enthalpy of formation from combustion

cards.title: $\ce{N2 + O2 -> 2NO}$, $\Delta H = +180.5\,\mathrm{kJ}$; $\ce{2NO + O2 -> 2NO2}$, $\Delta H = -114.1\,\mathrm{kJ}$. What is $\Delta H$ in kJ for $\ce{N2 + 2O2 -> 2NO2}$?
cards.body:
66.4

The two steps add directly, and $2\ce{NO}$ cancels: $180.5 + (-114.1) = +66.4\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

The positive sign means forming $\ce{NO2}$ from its elements is endothermic.
cards.searchQuery: Hess's law N2 O2 NO2 enthalpy change two steps

cards.title: Bond enthalpies (kJ/mol): H-H 436, Cl-Cl 243, H-Cl 431. Estimate $\Delta H$ in kJ for $\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}$.
cards.body:
-183

$\Delta H \approx \sum(\text{bonds broken}) - \sum(\text{bonds formed}) = (436 + 243) - 2(431) = 679 - 862$.

Watch out: this is **broken minus formed**, the reverse of the $\Delta H_f$ rule (products minus reactants).
cards.searchQuery: estimate reaction enthalpy from bond enthalpies H2 Cl2 HCl

cards.title: Is breaking a chemical bond exothermic or endothermic?
cards.body:
endothermic

Energy must be **supplied** to pull atoms apart, while forming a bond releases the same energy.

A reaction is exothermic overall when the bonds formed are stronger than the bonds broken.
cards.searchQuery: bond breaking endothermic bond formation exothermic

cards.title: $\Delta H_{\mathrm{fus}}$ of water is $6.01\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. How much heat, in kJ, melts $36.0\,\mathrm{g}$ of ice at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$? ($M = 18.0\,\mathrm{g/mol}$)
cards.body:
12.0

$n = 36.0 / 18.0 = 2.00\,\mathrm{mol}$, so $q = n\Delta H_{\mathrm{fus}} = 2.00 \times 6.01 = 12.0\,\mathrm{kJ}$.

The temperature stays at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ during melting; all the heat goes into breaking intermolecular attractions.
cards.searchQuery: heat of fusion ice calculation enthalpy of fusion water

cards.title: Why is the temperature constant on the flat parts of a heating curve?
cards.body:
The added heat is breaking **intermolecular attractions** (a phase change), not raising kinetic energy.

The temperature starts rising again only when the whole sample has changed phase.

Example: while ice melts at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, the ice-water mixture stays at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
cards.searchQuery: heating curve plateau phase change constant temperature

cards.title: Why is $\Delta H_{\mathrm{vap}}$ much larger than $\Delta H_{\mathrm{fus}}$ for the same substance?
cards.body:
Vaporization separates the molecules **completely**, while melting only loosens them.

For water, $\Delta H_{\mathrm{vap}} = 40.7\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta H_{\mathrm{fus}} = 6.01\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$.

Key idea: in the liquid, most intermolecular attractions are still present.
cards.searchQuery: why enthalpy of vaporization larger than enthalpy of fusion

cards.title: What does the second law of thermodynamics say about $\Delta S_{\mathrm{univ}}$ for a spontaneous process?
cards.body:
$\Delta S_{\mathrm{univ}} > 0$

The entropy of the universe, $\Delta S_{\mathrm{univ}} = \Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}} + \Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}}$, increases in every spontaneous process.

Watch out: the **system's** entropy can decrease, as when water freezes, as long as the surroundings gain more.
cards.searchQuery: second law of thermodynamics entropy of universe increases spontaneous

cards.title: What does the third law of thermodynamics say about a perfect crystal at $0\,\mathrm{K}$?
cards.body:
Its entropy is **zero**.

That gives entropy an absolute zero point, so tables list absolute molar entropies $S^\circ$, which are always positive above $0\,\mathrm{K}$.

Watch out: unlike $\Delta H^\circ_f$ of an element, the $S^\circ$ of an element is **not** zero at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.
cards.searchQuery: third law of thermodynamics perfect crystal zero entropy absolute

cards.title: What does Boltzmann's equation $S = k_B\ln W$ say about entropy?
cards.body:
Entropy measures the number of **microstates** $W$ available to a system.

More ways to arrange the energy and particles means higher entropy; $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant.

Key idea: entropy counts the number of microscopic arrangements consistent with the macroscopic state.
cards.searchQuery: Boltzmann entropy S = k ln W microstates meaning

cards.title: Which has the larger standard molar entropy at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $\ce{CH4(g)}$ or $\ce{C2H6(g)}$?
cards.body:
$\ce{C2H6(g)}$

Larger, more complex molecules have more ways to rotate and vibrate, so more accessible microstates.

Tip: for similar phases, entropy rises with molar mass and molecular complexity.
cards.searchQuery: standard molar entropy comparison methane ethane molecular complexity

cards.title: $S^\circ$ in J/(mol K): $\ce{N2}$ 191.6, $\ce{H2}$ 130.7, $\ce{NH3}$ 192.5. What is $\Delta S^\circ$ in J/K for $\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}$?
cards.body:
-198.7

$\Delta S^\circ = \sum nS^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum nS^\circ(\text{reactants}) = 2(192.5) - [191.6 + 3(130.7)] = 385.0 - 583.7$.

The negative sign agrees with 4 mol of gas becoming 2 mol.

Watch out: multiply each $S^\circ$ by its coefficient.
cards.searchQuery: standard entropy change reaction calculation ammonia synthesis

cards.title: A reaction has $\Delta H = -92.2\,\mathrm{kJ}$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$. What is $\Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}}$ in J/K (nearest whole number)?
cards.body:
309

$\Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}} = -\Delta H/T = +92{,}200\,\mathrm{J}/298\,\mathrm{K} = +309\,\mathrm{J/K}$.

An exothermic reaction dumps heat into the surroundings, raising their entropy.

Watch out: convert kJ to J so the units match J/K.
cards.searchQuery: entropy change of surroundings -ΔH/T calculation

cards.title: At $298\,\mathrm{K}$, a reaction has $\Delta H^\circ = -92.2\,\mathrm{kJ}$ and $\Delta S^\circ = -198.7\,\mathrm{J/K}$. What is $\Delta G^\circ$ in kJ?
cards.body:
-33.0

$\Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ = -92.2\,\mathrm{kJ} - (298)(-0.1987\,\mathrm{kJ/K}) = -92.2 + 59.2$.

Watch out: express $\Delta S$ in **kJ/K** (divide J by 1000) before combining with $\Delta H$.
cards.searchQuery: calculate delta G from delta H and delta S at 298 K

cards.title: A reaction has $\Delta H = +160\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta S = +200\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$. Above what temperature in kelvin is it spontaneous?
cards.body:
800

Set $\Delta G = 0$: $T = \Delta H/\Delta S = 160{,}000/200 = 800\,\mathrm{K}$.

Because $\Delta S > 0$, the $-T\Delta S$ term wins at higher $T$ and $\Delta G < 0$ above this temperature.

Watch out: convert $\Delta H$ to joules to match $\Delta S$.
cards.searchQuery: temperature at which reaction becomes spontaneous delta H over delta S

cards.title: How does $\Delta G$ at non-standard conditions relate to $\Delta G^\circ$ and $Q$?
cards.body:
$\Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q$

The sign of $\Delta G$ (not $\Delta G^\circ$) decides the actual direction: negative means forward.

At equilibrium, $\Delta G = 0$ and $Q = K$, which gives $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$.

Watch out: $\Delta G^\circ$ only tells you about the standard state ($Q = 1$).
cards.searchQuery: delta G equals delta G standard plus RT ln Q nonstandard

cards.title: What is the value of $\Delta G$ (not $\Delta G^\circ$) for a system at equilibrium, in kJ/mol?
cards.body:
0

At equilibrium there is no driving force in either direction, and $Q = K$.

Watch out: $\Delta G^\circ$ is zero at equilibrium only when $K = 1$.
cards.searchQuery: Gibbs free energy at equilibrium delta G equals zero

cards.title: A reaction has $K = 1.0 \times 10^5$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$. What is $\Delta G^\circ$ in kJ/mol, to three significant figures?
cards.body:
-28.5

$\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -(8.314)(298)\ln(10^5) = -(2478)(11.51) = -28{,}500\,\mathrm{J/mol}$.

Tip: $\Delta G^\circ \approx -5.71\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ for each factor of 10 in $K$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$, and $5 \times 5.71 = 28.5$.
cards.searchQuery: calculate delta G standard from equilibrium constant K = 1e5

cards.title: A reaction has $\Delta G^\circ = +10.0\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ at $298\,\mathrm{K}$. What is $K$, to two significant figures?
cards.body:
0.018

$\ln K = -\dfrac{10{,}000}{(8.314)(298)} = -4.04$, so $K = e^{-4.04} = 0.018$.

A positive $\Delta G^\circ$ means $K < 1$: reactants are favored at equilibrium.

Watch out: $K < 1$ does not mean no products form, only that they are a minority.
cards.searchQuery: equilibrium constant from positive standard Gibbs energy calculation

cards.title: Does a negative $\Delta G$ mean a reaction is fast?
cards.body:
No: $\Delta G$ says whether a reaction can occur, not **how fast**.

Diamond turning into graphite has $\Delta G < 0$ but is immeasurably slow because of its high activation energy.

Key idea: thermodynamics gives direction and extent; kinetics gives speed.
cards.searchQuery: spontaneous does not mean fast thermodynamics versus kinetics diamond graphite

cards.title: Dissolving $\ce{NH4NO3}$ in water is endothermic yet spontaneous. What drives it?
cards.body:
An **increase in entropy** ($\Delta S > 0$).

The ordered solid breaks into free ions in solution. At room temperature the $-T\Delta S$ term outweighs the positive $\Delta H$, so $\Delta G < 0$.

Key idea: $\Delta H > 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$ is spontaneous at high enough $T$.
cards.searchQuery: endothermic dissolution spontaneous entropy driven ammonium nitrate

cards.title: For water, $\Delta H_{\mathrm{vap}} = 40.7\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta S_{\mathrm{vap}} = 109\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$. Estimate the normal boiling point in kelvin.
cards.body:
373

At the boiling point liquid and gas are in equilibrium, so $\Delta G = 0$ and $T = \Delta H/\Delta S = 40{,}700/109 = 373\,\mathrm{K}$.

That's $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

Watch out: use $\Delta H$ in joules to match $\Delta S$.
cards.searchQuery: boiling point from enthalpy and entropy of vaporization water

cards.title: A galvanic cell reaction with $n = 2$ has $\Delta G^\circ = -193\,\mathrm{kJ}$. What is $E^\circ_{\mathrm{cell}}$ in volts, to three significant figures?
cards.body:
1.00

$E^\circ = -\Delta G^\circ/(nF) = 193{,}000\,\mathrm{J}/[(2)(96{,}485\,\mathrm{C/mol})] = 1.00\,\mathrm{V}$.

Watch out: use $\Delta G^\circ$ in joules.
cards.searchQuery: cell potential from delta G standard E = -ΔG/nF calculation

cards.title: At $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, a cell reaction has $n = 2$ and $E^\circ = 0.0592\,\mathrm{V}$. What is $K$?
cards.body:
100

At $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, $\log K = \dfrac{nE^\circ}{0.0592\,\mathrm{V}} = \dfrac{2(0.0592)}{0.0592} = 2$, so $K = 10^2$.

This comes from $nFE^\circ = RT\ln K$.

Tip: every $0.0296\,\mathrm{V}$ of $E^\circ$ (for $n = 2$) multiplies $K$ by 10.
cards.searchQuery: equilibrium constant from standard cell potential log K = nE/0.0592

cards.title: Write the Nernst equation at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for a cell with $n$ electrons transferred.
cards.body:
$E = E^\circ - \dfrac{0.0592}{n}\log Q$

It gives the cell potential at any concentrations; at equilibrium $Q = K$ and $E = 0$.

In general form, $E = E^\circ - \dfrac{RT}{nF}\ln Q$.

Tip: when $Q < 1$ (more reactants), $E > E^\circ$.
cards.searchQuery: Nernst equation cell potential non-standard concentrations 0.0592

cards.title: How is the rate of $\ce{aA -> products}$ defined in terms of the concentration of A, and in what units?
cards.body:
Rate $= -\dfrac{1}{a}\dfrac{\Delta[\ce{A}]}{\Delta t}$, in $\mathrm{M/s}$

The minus sign makes the rate positive, because a reactant's concentration falls.

Dividing by the coefficient $a$ makes the rate the same for every species in the reaction.

Watch out: for a product, the rate is $+\Delta[\ce{P}]/\Delta t$ divided by its coefficient.
cards.searchQuery: definition of reaction rate change in concentration over time stoichiometry

cards.title: How do you find the instantaneous rate at time $t$ from a plot of concentration versus time?
cards.body:
Take the **slope of the tangent** to the curve at that time, and use its magnitude.

The **initial rate** is the slope at $t = 0$. An average rate uses $\Delta[\ce{A}]/\Delta t$ over a whole interval.

Tip: initial rates are used in the method of initial rates because the products haven't built up yet.
cards.searchQuery: instantaneous rate tangent slope concentration time graph initial rate

cards.title: In $\ce{2N2O5 -> 4NO2 + O2}$, $\ce{N2O5}$ disappears at $0.020\,\mathrm{M/s}$. At what rate in M/s does $\ce{O2}$ form?
cards.body:
0.010

Rate $= -\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\Delta[\ce{N2O5}]}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{\Delta[\ce{O2}]}{\Delta t}$, so $\ce{O2}$ forms at half the rate $\ce{N2O5}$ is consumed.

For comparison, $\ce{NO2}$ forms at $0.040\,\mathrm{M/s}$.

Tip: scale each species' rate by the ratio of coefficients.
cards.searchQuery: relative rates of formation and disappearance stoichiometry N2O5

cards.title: What does the rate constant $k$ depend on, and what does it not depend on?
cards.body:
$k$ depends on **temperature** and on the catalyst (and the reaction itself), but **not** on concentrations.

Concentrations enter through the rate law factors, such as $[\ce{A}]^m$.

Key idea: $k$ is constant at a fixed temperature, which is why it can be compared between experiments.
cards.searchQuery: rate constant depends on temperature not concentration catalyst

cards.title: A reaction has rate $= k[\ce{A}]^2[\ce{B}]$. What is the overall order?
cards.body:
3

The overall order is the **sum** of the exponents: $2 + 1 = 3$.

It is second order in A, first order in B, and third order overall.
cards.searchQuery: overall reaction order sum of exponents rate law

cards.title: What are the units of $k$ for a first-order reaction, if time is in seconds?
cards.body:
1/s

Rate has units $\mathrm{M/s}$ and the rate law is rate $= k[\ce{A}]$, so $k$ must be $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.

General rule: for overall order $n$, $k$ has units $\mathrm{M^{1-n}\,s^{-1}}$.
cards.searchQuery: units of rate constant first order reaction per second

cards.title: What are the units of $k$ for a reaction that is second order overall (concentration in M, time in s)?
cards.body:
$\mathrm{M^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$

Rate $= k[\ce{A}]^2$ means $k = \mathrm{M/s} \div \mathrm{M^2}$.

The same units apply to $k[\ce{A}][\ce{B}]$, which is also second order overall.
cards.searchQuery: units of rate constant second order reaction M^-1 s^-1

cards.title: What are the units of $k$ for a zero-order reaction (concentration in M, time in s)?
cards.body:
M/s

Rate $= k[\ce{A}]^0 = k$, so $k$ has the same units as the rate.
cards.searchQuery: units of rate constant zero order reaction M/s

cards.title: Rate $= k[\ce{A}]^m[\ce{B}]^n$. Runs $([\ce{A}], [\ce{B}], \text{rate})$: $(0.10, 0.10, 2.0 \times 10^{-3})$, $(0.20, 0.10, 4.0 \times 10^{-3})$, $(0.10, 0.20, 8.0 \times 10^{-3})$. Find $n$.
cards.body:
2

Runs 1 and 3 change only $[\ce{B}]$: doubling it makes the rate **4 times** larger, so $2^n = 4$ and $n = 2$.

Runs 1 and 2 change only $[\ce{A}]$: doubling it doubles the rate, so $m = 1$.

Tip: always compare two runs in which only one concentration changes.
cards.searchQuery: method of initial rates data table find order in B

cards.title: For $\ce{A + B -> P}$ with rate $= k[\ce{A}][\ce{B}]^2$, a run at $[\ce{A}] = [\ce{B}] = 0.10\,\mathrm{M}$ has rate $2.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{M/s}$. Find $k$ in $\mathrm{M^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$.
cards.body:
2.0

$k = \dfrac{\text{rate}}{[\ce{A}][\ce{B}]^2} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-3}}{(0.10)(0.10)^2} = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-3}}{1.0 \times 10^{-3}}$.

Watch out: the units follow the order: third order overall gives $\mathrm{M^{-2}\,s^{-1}}$.
cards.searchQuery: calculate rate constant k from initial rate and rate law

cards.title: A first-order reaction has $k = 0.0300\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. What percent of A remains after $50.0\,\mathrm{s}$? Number only, three significant figures.
cards.body:
22.3

$\ln\dfrac{[\ce{A}]_t}{[\ce{A}]_0} = -kt = -(0.0300)(50.0) = -1.50$, so the fraction left is $e^{-1.50} = 0.223$.

Watch out: the exponent is $-kt$, with the minus sign, since A is decaying.
cards.searchQuery: first order integrated rate law fraction remaining calculation

cards.title: A first-order reaction has $t_{1/2} = 20.0\,\mathrm{min}$. How many minutes until 75% of the reactant has been consumed?
cards.body:
40.0

75% consumed means 25% remains, which is two half-lives: $100\% \to 50\% \to 25\%$.

So $t = 2 \times 20.0 = 40.0\,\mathrm{min}$.

Watch out: don't add 75% to 25%; count how many halvings it takes to get to what is left.
cards.searchQuery: first order half-lives number to reach 75 percent consumed

cards.title: A first-order reaction has $t_{1/2} = 35.0\,\mathrm{min}$. What is $k$ in $\mathrm{min^{-1}}$, to three significant figures?
cards.body:
0.0198

$k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{t_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{35.0}$.

Tip: the two forms of the same relationship are $t_{1/2} = 0.693/k$ and $k = 0.693/t_{1/2}$.
cards.searchQuery: first order rate constant from half-life ln 2 divided by t half

cards.title: A sample has $80.0\,\mathrm{g}$ of a radioisotope. How many grams remain after three half-lives?
cards.body:
10.0

Radioactive decay is first order: each half-life halves the amount, $80.0 \to 40.0 \to 20.0 \to 10.0\,\mathrm{g}$.

Equivalently, $80.0 \times (1/2)^3 = 10.0\,\mathrm{g}$.
cards.searchQuery: radioactive decay half-life remaining amount after three half-lives

cards.title: A zero-order reaction has $[\ce{A}]_0 = 0.80\,\mathrm{M}$ and $k = 0.020\,\mathrm{M/s}$. What is its half-life in seconds?
cards.body:
20

For zero order, $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[\ce{A}]_0}{2k} = \dfrac{0.80}{2(0.020)}$.

The half-life of a zero-order reaction is **proportional** to $[\ce{A}]_0$: it shrinks as the reaction goes on.

Watch out: don't use $\ln 2/k$; that is first order only.
cards.searchQuery: zero order half-life formula A0 over 2k calculation

cards.title: A second-order reaction has $k = 0.50\,\mathrm{M^{-1}\,s^{-1}}$ and $[\ce{A}]_0 = 0.20\,\mathrm{M}$. What is its half-life in seconds?
cards.body:
10

$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{1}{k[\ce{A}]_0} = \dfrac{1}{(0.50)(0.20)} = 10\,\mathrm{s}$.

The half-life of a second-order reaction **grows** as the reaction proceeds, because $[\ce{A}]$ falls.
cards.searchQuery: second order half-life formula 1 over k A0 calculation

cards.title: Write the integrated rate law for a reaction that is second order in A.
cards.body:
$\dfrac{1}{[\ce{A}]_t} = kt + \dfrac{1}{[\ce{A}]_0}$

A plot of $1/[\ce{A}]$ against $t$ is a straight line with slope $+k$.

Tip: unlike first order, the line **rises** because $1/[\ce{A}]$ grows as A is consumed.
cards.searchQuery: second order integrated rate law 1/[A] versus time

cards.title: Write the integrated rate law for a zero-order reaction, and say when zero-order behavior occurs.
cards.body:
$[\ce{A}]_t = [\ce{A}]_0 - kt$

The concentration falls linearly with slope $-k$.

Zero order shows up when something other than $[\ce{A}]$ limits the rate, such as a **saturated catalyst surface** or enzyme.
cards.searchQuery: zero order integrated rate law linear decay saturated catalyst

cards.title: What is a pseudo-first-order reaction, and how is it created?
cards.body:
A reaction whose rate depends on **one** concentration because the other reactant is in large excess.

If $[\ce{B}]$ is huge, it stays essentially constant, so rate $= k[\ce{A}][\ce{B}] \approx k'[\ce{A}]$ with $k' = k[\ce{B}]$.

Tip: chemists use this trick to measure the order in a single reactant.
cards.searchQuery: pseudo-first-order reaction excess reagent constant concentration

cards.title: A plot of $1/[\ce{A}]$ versus time is a straight line. What is the order of the reaction in A?
cards.body:
second

$1/[\ce{A}]$ versus $t$ is linear only for **second-order** kinetics, with slope $+k$.

Mnemonic: zero order uses $[\ce{A}]$, first order uses $\ln[\ce{A}]$, second order uses $1/[\ce{A}]$.
cards.searchQuery: integrated rate law plots zero first second order linear 1/[A]

cards.title: According to collision theory, what two conditions must a collision meet to cause a reaction?
cards.body:
The molecules must collide with at least the **activation energy** and with the proper **orientation**.

Most collisions fail one of the two, which is why reactions are much slower than the collision frequency alone would suggest.

Key idea: energy and geometry both matter.
cards.searchQuery: collision theory sufficient energy proper orientation reaction rate

cards.title: What is the activation energy of a reaction?
cards.body:
The **minimum energy** colliding molecules need for a reaction to occur: the height of the energy barrier above the reactants.

On an energy diagram it is the peak (transition state) minus the energy of the reactants.

Watch out: $E_a$ is not $\Delta H$; a reaction can be strongly exothermic and still have a large $E_a$.
cards.searchQuery: activation energy definition energy barrier transition state reactants

cards.title: Why does raising the temperature speed up a reaction so much more than the increase in collision frequency alone would suggest?
cards.body:
The **fraction of molecules with energy of at least $E_a$** rises sharply.

That fraction grows exponentially, as in $e^{-E_a/RT}$, while the collision frequency grows only slightly with $T$.

Tip: a rough rule is that the rate doubles for each $10\,\mathrm{K}$ rise near room temperature (for $E_a \approx 50\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$).
cards.searchQuery: temperature effect on reaction rate fraction of molecules above activation energy

cards.title: Why does increasing the concentration of a reactant usually increase the rate?
cards.body:
More molecules per volume means more **collisions per second**, so more successful collisions.

The size of the effect, however, is set by the reaction order and found by experiment.

Watch out: a zero-order reactant does not speed up the reaction at all.
cards.searchQuery: concentration effect on reaction rate collision frequency

cards.title: Why does a powdered solid react faster than the same mass of a single lump?
cards.body:
Powder has far more **exposed surface area**, so more reactant particles can collide at once.

This is the rate-limiting factor for reactions at a solid surface.

Example: finely divided flour dust can ignite explosively, while a bag of flour will not.
cards.searchQuery: surface area effect on reaction rate powder versus lump

cards.title: Write the Arrhenius equation for the rate constant $k$.
cards.body:
$k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}$

$A$ is the frequency (pre-exponential) factor, $E_a$ the activation energy, $R = 8.314\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$ and $T$ the absolute temperature.

Bigger $E_a$ or lower $T$ makes $k$ smaller.

Watch out: use $E_a$ in joules per mole with $R$ in joules.
cards.searchQuery: Arrhenius equation k = A e^(-Ea/RT) activation energy

cards.title: What does the frequency factor $A$ in the Arrhenius equation represent?
cards.body:
The rate of collisions with the **correct orientation**, effectively $k$ if every such collision had enough energy.

It combines the collision frequency with a steric (orientation) factor and is nearly independent of $T$.

Key idea: $A$ sets the maximum possible $k$; the exponential factor is the fraction of collisions energetic enough.
cards.searchQuery: Arrhenius frequency factor pre-exponential collision frequency orientation

cards.title: A rate constant exactly doubles when $T$ rises from $300\,\mathrm{K}$ to $310\,\mathrm{K}$. What is $E_a$ in kJ/mol, to three significant figures?
cards.body:
53.6

$\ln 2 = \dfrac{E_a}{R}\left(\dfrac{1}{300} - \dfrac{1}{310}\right) = \dfrac{E_a}{8.314}(1.075 \times 10^{-4})$.

So $E_a = \dfrac{(0.6931)(8.314)}{1.075 \times 10^{-4}} = 5.36 \times 10^4\,\mathrm{J/mol}$.

Watch out: give the answer in kJ, and use kelvin in the temperature terms.
cards.searchQuery: calculate activation energy from rate constants at two temperatures

cards.title: A reaction has $E_a = 50.0\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$. By what factor does $k$ increase from $300\,\mathrm{K}$ to $310\,\mathrm{K}$? Give three significant figures.
cards.body:
1.91

$\ln\dfrac{k_2}{k_1} = \dfrac{E_a}{R}\left(\dfrac{1}{T_1} - \dfrac{1}{T_2}\right) = \dfrac{50{,}000}{8.314}(1.075 \times 10^{-4}) = 0.647$.

Then $k_2/k_1 = e^{0.647} = 1.91$.

Tip: this matches the rule of thumb that a $10\,\mathrm{K}$ rise roughly doubles the rate.
cards.searchQuery: Arrhenius equation ratio of rate constants 300 K to 310 K Ea 50 kJ

cards.title: An Arrhenius plot of $\ln k$ versus $1/T$ has slope $-6.00 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{K}$. What is $E_a$ in kJ/mol, to three significant figures?
cards.body:
49.9

$E_a = -\text{slope} \times R = (6.00 \times 10^3\,\mathrm{K})(8.314\,\mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}) = 49{,}900\,\mathrm{J/mol}$.

Watch out: the slope is negative, but $E_a$ is positive.
cards.searchQuery: activation energy from Arrhenius plot slope times R

cards.title: What is the molecularity of the elementary step $\ce{NO2 + NO2 -> NO3 + NO}$?
cards.body:
bimolecular

Molecularity is the number of reactant particles that collide in an elementary step: 1 is unimolecular, 2 bimolecular, 3 termolecular.

Watch out: molecularity applies only to **elementary** steps, never to an overall reaction.
cards.searchQuery: molecularity of elementary step bimolecular unimolecular termolecular

cards.title: What is the rate law for the elementary step $\ce{A + B -> C}$?
cards.body:
$\text{rate} = k[\ce{A}][\ce{B}]$

For an **elementary** step the exponents equal the coefficients, because the rate depends on how often the particles meet.

Watch out: this shortcut is not valid for an overall reaction whose mechanism is unknown.
cards.searchQuery: rate law for elementary bimolecular step coefficients are exponents

cards.title: What is the rate law for the elementary step $\ce{A -> products}$?
cards.body:
$\text{rate} = k[\ce{A}]$

A unimolecular step is first order in its single reactant.

Key idea: elementary-step rate laws follow directly from the molecularity.
cards.searchQuery: unimolecular elementary step first order rate law

cards.title: Why are termolecular elementary steps rare in mechanisms?
cards.body:
The chance of **three** particles colliding at the same moment with the right energy and orientation is very small.

Most mechanisms use unimolecular and bimolecular steps.

Tip: a third-order overall rate law usually signals a multistep mechanism, such as one with a fast pre-equilibrium.
cards.searchQuery: why termolecular steps are rare three body collision mechanism

cards.title: How do you tell an intermediate from a catalyst in a mechanism?
cards.body:
An **intermediate** is formed in one step and consumed in a later step; a **catalyst** is consumed in an early step and regenerated in a later one.

Neither appears in the overall equation.

Mnemonic: an intermediate is produced then used; a catalyst is used then produced.
cards.searchQuery: intermediate versus catalyst difference mechanism

cards.title: What two conditions must a proposed mechanism satisfy?
cards.body:
The steps must **sum to the overall equation**, and the rate law from the slow step must **match the experimental rate law**.

A mechanism can be ruled out by data but never proven by it.

Key idea: agreement with experiment is necessary, not sufficient.
cards.searchQuery: mechanism requirements sum to overall equation rate law agrees with experiment

cards.title: $\ce{2NO <=> N2O2}$ is fast and reversible, then $\ce{N2O2 + O2 -> 2NO2}$ is slow. What rate law does this mechanism predict?
cards.body:
$\text{rate} = k[\ce{NO}]^2[\ce{O2}]$

The slow step gives rate $= k_2[\ce{N2O2}][\ce{O2}]$, but $\ce{N2O2}$ is an intermediate.

The fast pre-equilibrium gives $[\ce{N2O2}] = K[\ce{NO}]^2$, so $k = k_2K$.

Tip: replace each intermediate in the slow-step rate law using the fast equilibrium before it.
cards.searchQuery: fast pre-equilibrium mechanism rate law NO O2 intermediate elimination

cards.title: On a reaction energy diagram, what is the difference between a transition state and an intermediate?
cards.body:
A **transition state** is the energy maximum (a peak) along a step; an **intermediate** is a local minimum (a valley) between two steps.

Intermediates can sometimes be detected; transition states exist only fleetingly.

Tip: in a multistep mechanism, the step with the highest peak is the rate-determining step.
cards.searchQuery: reaction energy diagram transition state peak intermediate valley

cards.title: A reaction has $E_a = 85\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ forward and $120\,\mathrm{kJ/mol}$ reverse. What is $\Delta H$ in kJ/mol for the forward reaction?
cards.body:
-35

$\Delta H = E_{a,\mathrm{fwd}} - E_{a,\mathrm{rev}} = 85 - 120$.

The products lie below the reactants on the energy diagram, so the reaction is exothermic.
cards.searchQuery: delta H from forward and reverse activation energies energy diagram

cards.title: What is the difference between a homogeneous and a heterogeneous catalyst?
cards.body:
A **homogeneous** catalyst is in the same phase as the reactants; a **heterogeneous** catalyst is in a different phase, usually a solid.

Example: platinum, palladium and rhodium in a car's catalytic converter are heterogeneous, working on gases at the metal surface.
cards.searchQuery: homogeneous versus heterogeneous catalyst catalytic converter

cards.title: Can a catalyst appear in a reaction's rate law even though it is not in the overall equation?
cards.body:
Yes.

A catalyst takes part in the mechanism, so its concentration can affect the rate. Example: acid-catalyzed reactions often have rate $= k[\ce{H+}][\ce{reactant}]$.

The catalyst cancels out of the overall equation because it is regenerated.
cards.searchQuery: catalyst appears in rate law acid catalyzed reaction

cards.title: In $\ce{Cl + O3 -> ClO + O2}$ followed by $\ce{ClO + O -> Cl + O2}$, which species is the catalyst and which is the intermediate?
cards.body:
$\ce{Cl}$ is the catalyst; $\ce{ClO}$ is the intermediate.

$\ce{Cl}$ is consumed in the first step and regenerated in the second. $\ce{ClO}$ is formed in the first step and used up in the second.

The overall reaction is $\ce{O3 + O -> 2O2}$.
cards.searchQuery: chlorine radical catalyst ozone depletion mechanism intermediate ClO

cards.title: How do enzymes speed up biochemical reactions, and do they change the equilibrium?
cards.body:
They bind the substrate at the **active site**, stabilizing the transition state and lowering $E_a$.

They do **not** change $\Delta G$ or $K$, so the equilibrium position is the same; equilibrium is just reached faster.

Key idea: enzymes are catalysts, so they obey the same rules.
cards.searchQuery: enzyme catalysis lowers activation energy active site does not change equilibrium

cards.title: A $25.0\,\mathrm{g}$ metal at $100.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ goes into $100.0\,\mathrm{g}$ of water at $20.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$; both reach $22.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Find the metal's $c$ in J/(g°C).
cards.body:
0.54

Heat gained by water: $(100.0)(4.184)(2.5) = 1046\,\mathrm{J}$.

Heat lost by the metal equals this, with $\Delta T = 100.0 - 22.5 = 77.5\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$: $c = \dfrac{1046}{(25.0)(77.5)}$.

Watch out: the metal's $\Delta T$ is its own temperature drop, not the water's rise.
cards.searchQuery: calorimetry specific heat of unknown metal dropped in water calculation

cards.title: What is the sign of $\Delta S$ for $\ce{H2O(l) -> H2O(g)}$?
cards.body:
positive

A gas has far more accessible microstates than a liquid, since its molecules move freely through a much larger volume.

So vaporization always has $\Delta S > 0$, which is why boiling is favored at **high** temperature.
cards.searchQuery: entropy change vaporization liquid to gas positive
